claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 atomic percent yttrium to the refractory high-entropy alloy enhances radiation tolerance.
The yttrium addition promotes formation of nanometer-scale yttrium-rich oxide dispersoids.
The yttrium-rich oxide dispersoids serve as irradiation-defect sinks.
Adding 1–2 atomic percent yttrium preserves the alloy's mechanical integrity and processing practicality under plasma-facing conditions.
The baseline alloy consists of refractory elements such as Mo, Nb, Ta, W, and V, with no added reactive elements or engineered oxide dispersoids.
The yttrium-rich oxide dispersoids form both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Stable oxide dispersoids form during alloy processing as a result of yttrium addition.
The dispersoids absorb irradiation-induced point defects and dislocation loops.
Defect absorption by the dispersoids promotes defect recombination and reduces accumulated radiation damage.
The yttrium-modified alloy will exhibit approximately 20% or greater reduction in dislocation-loop density relative to the unmodified alloy.
The yttrium-modified alloy will retain at least 90% of its initial yield strength after irradiation.
The beneficial effect will hold during irradiation at 300–600°C and at fluxes relevant to plasma-facing fusion components.
Yttrium contents above 2–3 atomic percent may cause embrittlement or phase instability and negate the benefit.
The magnitude of improvement and uniformity of dispersoid formation depend on processing parameters and the starting microstructure.
Baseline and 1–2 atomic percent yttrium-modified samples will be irradiated under identical conditions and compared by TEM and mechanical testing.
The hypothesis is declared falsified only if defect-density improvement is less than approximately 20% and mechanical degradation exceeds 10% relative to the baseline.

contradictions.description: Mechanical integrity uses inconsistent comparators: the prediction requires retention of at least 90% of the modified alloy's own initial yield strength, whereas the falsification rule evaluates degradation relative to the irradiated baseline alloy.

The falsification rule requires both inadequate defect reduction and excessive mechanical degradation. Consequently, failure of either individual predicted outcome alone would not falsify the hypothesis, despite both being stated as required outcomes.
